media:group.media:description:
Street Cloud: AI-Powered Participatory Street Co-Design
Presented at the 4th IOER Conference “Space & Transformation” (22–24 September 2026, Dresden, Germany).
Street Cloud integrates Urban Informatics, GIScience, and AI to support participatory street redesign. Citizens share their ideas and priorities, while AI generates redesign scenarios that communities and planners can collaboratively evaluate and refine.
Research Team: Sandaruwan Sankalpa Silva, Amila Jayasinghe, Chethika Abenayake, Niroshan Sanjaya, and Samith Madusanka.
Affiliations: Department of Town & Country Planning, University of Moratuwa | Smarmind Research Group | Urban Simulation Lab.
We gratefully acknowledge the support of the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation, DAAD, and Technische Universität Dresden.

entry.title: Teaching and Learning Urban Science, Urban Informatics and Planning : The 5-Step Framework

media:group.media:title: Teaching and Learning Urban Science, Urban Informatics and Planning : The 5-Step Framework
media:group.media:description: How do we prepare the next generation of urban professionals for the complexity of modern cities? This video examines the shift from traditional "design-first" project teaching to a scientific, evidence-based inquiry model. We dive into the "convergent science" approach that integrates urban science, computer science, and GIScience. Key Topics Covered:Moving beyond traditional design briefs to tackle ill-structured, real-world problems. How to use urban informatics and data science to drive planning decisions. A deep dive into the 5-step pedagogical framework used by the Urban Simulation Lab. Insights into transforming academic practice for the digital age of urban planning

entry.title: PjBL vs PBL: Which is Better for Urban Informatics and Planning?

media:group.media:title: PjBL vs PBL: Which is Better for Urban Informatics and Planning?
media:group.media:description: In this video, we break down the critical differences between Project-Based Learning (PjBL) and Problem-Based Learning (PBL) within the context of urban education. Based on a white paper from the University of Moratuwa, we explore why a problem-driven approach is essential for mastering complex urban systems. In this video, you will learn:The fundamental differences between PjBL and PBL. Why Problem-Based Learning is the future of Urban Informatics. The 5-step studio framework: Describe, Inquire, Model, Extract, and State. Real-world examples of how these methodologies are applied in urban planning studios.

entry.title: Why City Problems Can't Be Solved — And How to Structure Them

media:group.media:title: Why City Problems Can't Be Solved — And How to Structure Them
media:group.media:description:
Cities don't have neat problems — they have wicked ones.
Traffic, heatwaves, inequality, housing — these aren't puzzles with clean answers. They're complex, deeply interconnected, and constantly shifting. Traditional urban planning wasn't built for this. Urban Science is.
In this video, we break down how to turn overwhelming urban chaos into something you can actually work with — using the DIMES Framework:
🔷 Describe → Define the problem context 🔷 Inquire → Map stakeholders & effects 🔷 Model → Break it down functionally 🔷 Extract → Find the leverage points 🔷 State → Articulate the structured problem
📌 We also apply DIMES to a real case: Urban Heatwaves — one of the most dangerous and underestimated threats facing cities today.
And finally: How will AI reshape the way future urban scientists think, work, and solve?
🎓 Perfect for urban planners, data scientists, policy students, and anyone curious about the future of cities.
🔔 Subscribe for more on Urban Science, complex systems, and AI in cities.

entry.title: Teaching the Convergent City: A Competency Framework for Urban Informatics Educators

media:group.media:title: Teaching the Convergent City: A Competency Framework for Urban Informatics Educators
media:group.media:description: This Video explains that the main challenge in modern urban informatics education is not just updating the curriculum, but fundamentally transforming the academic staff who teach it . Faculty members typically specialize in single disciplines and rely on subjective professional experience to teach the design of traditional, static master plans .To fix this, the authors propose a "Convergent Faculty Competency Framework" and a professional development pathway to help educators transition into convergent experts . This framework trains faculty to embrace scientific urban reasoning (like urban scaling laws and space syntax), teach the design of dynamic, AI-assisted "living" urban systems (like digital twins), and replace conventional design studios with dual-mode Problem-Based Learning (PBL) studios that integrate both quantitative spatial science and community-driven, participative planning

entry.title: GeoNet - application for geospatial network centrality assessment

media:group.media:title: GeoNet - application for geospatial network centrality assessment
media:group.media:description:
GeoNet is a powerful, user-friendly tool designed for performing centrality analysis on geospatial networks. It enables researchers, and planners to evaluate the importance and influence of nodes and connections within spatial networks such as road systems and transportation infrastructure.
In this video, we explore how GeoNet integrates concepts from Geographic Information Systems and Network Science to deliver meaningful insights through spatial network data analysis. The tool supports multiple centrality measures, including degree connectivity, betweenness centrality, and closeness centrality, helping users identify critical nodes and paths efficiently.
